content: Methenamine is indicated for the prophylactic or suppressive treatment of frequently recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) when long-term therapy is deemed necessary. The recommended dosage for methenamine hippurate is 1 gram taken orally every 12 hours, while methenamine mandelate is dosed at 1 gram orally every 6 hours. In elderly patients, dosing should be approached cautiously, starting at the lower end of the dosing range due to the increased likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. Methenamine should not be co-administered with acetazolamide, as this combination may result in the formation of an insoluble precipitate in the urine, reducing the effectiveness of both agents. Similarly, methenamine is contraindicated with sulfonamides such as sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, and sulfisoxazole for the same reason—formation of insoluble urinary precipitates that diminish the efficacy of both drugs. Methenamine should also be avoided in combination with the cholera vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics, including methenamine, may interfere with the vaccine strain, reducing its effectiveness. Patients should not receive the cholera vaccine if they have taken oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Methenamine may decrease the effects of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. These products contain bacterial spores, and the concurrent use of antibacterial agents may reduce their efficacy. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Caution is advised when methenamine is used with pseudoephedrine, as urinary acidifying agents like methenamine may increase the urinary excretion of indirect-acting alpha/beta agonists, potentially lowering their serum concentrations. Similarly, methenamine may reduce the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering colonic bacterial flora necessary for drug activation. Co-administration with antibiotics may further decrease the efficacy of this combination. Methenamine use may cause adverse effects such as dysuria, gastric upset, nausea, rash, or hypersensitivity reactions, particularly in patients sensitive to methenamine or tartrazine (FD&C Yellow No. 5). It is important to monitor liver function tests (LFTs), especially in patients with a history of liver impairment. Methenamine is not recommended for use during pregnancy, particularly in the first and second trimesters, as its safety has not been established. Additionally, it may precipitate uric acid stones in patients with gout. Methenamine is excreted in breast milk, but no adverse effects have been documented in lactating individuals. Methenamine is primarily excreted in the urine, with approximately 90% eliminated within 24 hours. However, mandelic or hippuric acid, its metabolites, may accumulate in patients with severe renal impairment.
